# Registration Center, Load Balancing and Consistent Hashing

## Category

database / cache subtree. Node position: registration discovery, load balancing and consistent hashing as they deform in game long-connection scenarios — "the lifetime of an allocation result" is the core judgment of this layer.

## Definition


Once the number of services passes the scale of "a few instances behind one domain name", "who is where, which one do we send the request to" becomes an independent problem. The registration center answers the former, load balancing answers the latter, and consistent hashing guards the stability of allocation results as nodes are added and removed. Each of these three is a mature component on its own; what genuinely deserves discussion is their deformation in game long-connection scenarios — many intuitions carried over from web services stop working here.

## Problem

Once the number of services passes "a few instances behind one domain", "who is where, which one do we send the request to" becomes an independent problem, and web-service intuition fails here: load balancing is not continuous adjustment, it allocates only at the moment of connection establishment; failures are not discovered instantly, the heartbeat window is counted in tens of seconds; and the cost of adding or removing nodes is either a full cache invalidation or a full reconnection. Mixing in any of these intuitions at the wrong time scale pays its price on the day of scaling up or down.


### What a registration center solves is "addresses change"

In the single-machine era, process addresses barely changed, and hard-coding them in a configuration file was fine. After services exist, instances scale up, scale down, restart and drift at any moment, and any hard-coded address will expire on some release day. A registration center turns "which instances are alive" into a dynamic fact: a service reports itself at startup, deregisters at shutdown, is removed once its heartbeat drops, and what a consumer receives each time is the currently available instance list.

Its positioning usually has two boundaries:

- What it maintains is routing facts like "who is alive, where are they", not the values of business configuration.
- It is a cache of routing information, whose source is each service instance itself; when the registration center is briefly unavailable, existing calls often survive for a while on the local cache.

Stuffing business parameters, event switches and canary rules into a registration center is a common overreach. Short term it saves one configuration system; long term it churns two kinds of data with completely different change frequencies together, instance removal and parameter changes interfere with each other, and during troubleshooting you cannot even answer "what was just changed".

### Heartbeat and removal: failures are not discovered instantly

A registration center gives consumers an available list, but that list has lag. An instance crashing does not announce itself, and must wait for a heartbeat timeout before being removed; after removal, the consumer's local cache still has to wait for the next refresh cycle before updating. So between an instance dying and all traffic leaving it there is usually a window counted in tens of seconds.

This window determines several design orientations:

- The caller must handle the failure of "hitting a dead instance" itself; retries cannot rely entirely on the registration center.
- Heartbeat interval and removal threshold are a pair of tradeoffs: too fast and network jitter false-terminates, too slow and the failure window lengthens.
- Graceful shutdown matters far more than crash removal; proactively deregistering compresses the window from tens of seconds down to near zero.

In game scenarios this window is more glaring, because players immediately feel a long connection dropping. Deregistering from the list before release and waiting for connections to drain naturally is usually far more dignified than relying on heartbeat timeouts.

### Long connections strip real-time behavior from load balancing

Load balancing for web requests is a per-request decision: which instance gets this one, which gets the next, and it can be reshuffled at any time. Game long connections are not — at the moment a player connects, the allocation is already fixed, and all traffic over the following hours flows along that connection. Balancing is no longer an ongoing adjustment process but a one-shot allocation result.

This produces several phenomena that do not exist in web scenarios:

- The balance only reflects the state at connection time; afterwards instance loads drift naturally, and the late-peak distribution is entirely different from what it was at connection time.
- When a batch of players floods in at once, if allocation only looks at "current connection count", a newly online instance is instantly flooded full.
- Removing an instance is not as simple as deleting it from the list; you have to wait for the players attached to it to leave naturally or be actively migrated.

So game infrastructure load assessment usually reads the curve of "connection distribution plus drain rate", rather than a snapshot of connection count at some instant. The warm-up rhythm of new instances under an opening surge belongs to the same problem.

### Why session stickiness is almost the default in games

Session stickiness means requests from the same player session land on the same instance as much as possible. In a stateful game server this is not an optimization, it is a precondition: player sessions, room state and vision data all live in process memory, and switching instances means losing state. Even when the service itself is stateless, stickiness usually holds naturally in long-connection scenarios — where the connection is, the request goes.

The cost of stickiness also has to be acknowledged:

- Uneven allocation produces hot instances while other instances sit idle.
- When an instance fails, the players stuck on it must be migrated or reconnected as a block, and the impact is chunky rather than scattered.
- Releases can only roll at instance granularity, and every instance has to wait for its players to drain.

The common practice is to keep the scope of "stick" as small as possible: keep the gateway layer stateless, and let stickiness land only on the specific logic server or room server. That way the migration unit for failures and releases is one room or one region, not every connection on the whole gateway.

### What problem does consistent hashing actually solve

Ordinary hashing spreads keys across nodes, and the price is that whenever the node count changes, the ownership of almost every key is reshuffled. For a cache, one expansion equals one full cache invalidation; for a long-connection gateway, one expansion equals one full reconnection. Consistent hashing confines the impact of "node change" to neighboring segments: adding or removing a node moves only the keys between it and its neighbors on the ring, and everything else stays put.

Its suitable scenarios share several features:

- The key count is large and cannot tolerate an overall reshuffle, such as sessions, rooms, or sharded data.
- Nodes are added and removed frequently, and elastic scaling is the norm rather than a once-a-year accident.
- Allocation results must stay stable long term, so the same key recomputed repeatedly still lands on the same node.

Conversely, if the node set stays fixed for a long time and keys are stateless, ordinary hashing or plain round-robin is simpler. Consistent hashing is extra complexity, and whether it is worth introducing depends on "what would a reshuffle break".

### Virtual nodes and data skew

The original form of consistent hashing has an engineering problem: with few nodes, the ring's segments are partitioned close to randomly, and individual nodes may get a noticeably oversized segment. Virtual nodes are the common fix — each physical node expands into dozens or hundreds of virtual positions on the ring, and the segment distribution becomes even; when a node dies, the keys it carried are spread across several neighbors, rather than all dumped onto a single node.

Two more points usually deserve attention when using it:

- The quality of the hash function directly determines the distribution, and simple hand-rolled hashes on the business side often skew noticeably.
- When node specifications differ, the number of virtual nodes can be weighted proportionally, letting newer hardware share more load.

Further along there is the hot-key problem: consistent hashing only balances the number of keys, not their access volume. A few extremely hot rooms or a few high-spending players may all be crammed onto the same node on the ring, at which point you either add a random suffix at the key level to scatter them, or accept the hotspot and handle it separately.

### Common pitfalls

- Using a registration center as a configuration center, so instance removal and parameter changes interfere with each other.
- Assuming load balancing continuously adjusts traffic, when in long-connection scenarios allocation happens only at the moment of connection.
- Not assessing the reconnection cost before expanding, so one elastic scaling becomes one full disconnection.
- Tuning the heartbeat too fast, so network jitter is mistaken for node failure, and the removal storm knocks the callers over instead.
- Watching only the evenness of key counts, ignoring how hot keys reconcentrate traffic onto a single node.

The core judgment of this infrastructure layer is "the lifetime of an allocation result": request-level balancing, connection-level stickiness, and data-level hash rings each correspond to different time scales, and mixing in any of these intuitions pays its price on the day of scaling up or down.

## Used By

Registration discovery selection and boundaries after services exist (routing facts vs business configuration); load assessment for long-connection gateways (connection distribution + drain-rate curve); controlling the scope of session stickiness; deciding whether to introduce consistent hashing and virtual nodes.

## Related

Chain of relations: registration discovery (who is alive) → heartbeat removal window → load allocation (fixed at connection time) → session stickiness → consistent hashing (data-level stability). Upstream: service splitting of the server tree (server/services). Downstream: AOI (the server tree, the same class of "reshuffle cost" problem — adding and removing the visible set equally requires controlling jitter).

## Reference

The original consistent hashing paper: Karger et al., "Consistent Hashing and Random Trees" (STOC 1997); the rest of this page is a synthesis of engineering experience.
